title: How to Deal With Anger
excerpt: Anger is not the sin. What you do in the four seconds after the anger arrives is the sin, or the saint. The whole battle is fought in those four seconds.
body:
Anger has a bad reputation in the church, and it has earned some of it, but the Bible's view is more honest than ours. God himself is described as angry, repeatedly, at injustice and cruelty and the destruction of what he made. Jesus made a whip and cleared the temple. Paul wrote, be angry, and do not sin. Anger is not automatically wicked. It is an alarm. The question is never whether you will feel it. The question is what you will do with it, and that is where most of us fail.

I have done damage with my anger that took years to undo. Words said in ten seconds that lived in someone's memory for a decade. The problem was never that I felt angry. The problem was that I treated the feeling as a license, as if the heat I felt entitled me to whatever came next. It did not. It never does.

## Learn what your anger is telling you

Anger is a signal, and the first work is to read it instead of just discharging it. Anger usually fires when something we value is threatened, justice, respect, safety, control, our sense of being right. Sometimes the thing we value is good and the anger is righteous. Sometimes the thing we value is our own ego, and the anger is just pride defending itself with a loud voice.

So when the heat rises, before you act, ask one question. What do I think is being threatened right now? The answer tells you whether you are angry like God is angry, at real wrong, or angry like a child is angry, at not getting your way. Most of my anger, examined honestly, has been the second kind dressed up as the first.

## Win the four seconds

There is a small window between the spark of anger and the action it demands, and almost everything is decided there. The Bible's wisdom is full of this. Be slow to anger. A soft answer turns away wrath. He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty. The discipline is to insert a pause into the gap, to not act on the first impulse.

Practically, this means buying time. Take a breath before you speak. Say "give me a minute" and leave the room. Refuse to send the message tonight. The anger is loudest in the first moments and almost always quieter an hour later, and the quieter version makes far better decisions. Most of the damage anger does is done in the first sixty seconds, by a version of you that an hour later you would not recognize or approve.

## Do not feed it in the dark

Anger left alone in the mind does not cool. It rehearses. It builds the case, recalls every past offense, drafts the speech you will give, and by the time you finally speak you are angry not at the one thing but at a whole accumulated history. Paul said do not let the sun go down on your anger, and that is the cure. Do not carry it into the night to marinate. Deal with it the day it arrives, in the light, before it grows roots.

## Speak the anger instead of leaking it

There are two bad ways to handle anger, the explosion and the freeze. The explosion dumps it on people. The freeze buries it, where it turns into resentment, contempt, and a cold withdrawal that does as much damage as any shout. Neither is the way.

The better way is to speak it, honestly and without violence. To say, calmly, "I am angry about this, and here is why," and to deal with the actual issue. This takes more courage than either the blowup or the silence, because it requires you to be vulnerable about what hurt you instead of either attacking or hiding. But it is the only path that leads to anything resembling peace.

## Bring it to God before you bring it to the person

The psalms are full of raw anger spoken straight to God, including things you would be ashamed to say to anyone else. This is the model. Before you confront the person, take the anger to God. Tell him the whole ugly truth of it. Let him sort the righteous part from the prideful part. Often, by the time you have prayed it through, the anger has shrunk to its true size, and the conversation you go on to have is a human one instead of a war.

## When anger is a deeper pattern

For some, anger is not occasional but constant, an outsized rage that frightens the people they love, a pattern that breaks relationships and will not yield to ordinary effort. If that is you, especially if it has ever turned physical, the loving and faithful thing is to get help, a counselor, a pastor, an anger management program. Sometimes chronic anger sits on top of old wounds, trauma, or depression that need real treatment. Seeking that help is not weakness. It is the strongest thing such a person can do.

## This week

The next time anger rises, do one thing before anything else. Pause. Take a slow breath, say nothing for ten seconds, and ask yourself, what do I think is being threatened? Then, if the anger is still hot, delay any response by an hour and take it to God first. Practice the pause every single time anger flares this week, even over small things.

The anger will come. It always does. The only question is whether it gets the four seconds, or you do.
